Getting started with CFUestimatoR

CFUestimatoR.Rmd
library(CFUestimatoR)

Introduction

CFUestimatoR estimates colony forming units (CFU) from agar plate colony counts, using the maximum likelihood estimators from Martini et al. (2024). Please cite this paper if you use CFUestimatoR.

Martini KM, Boddu SS, Nemenman I, Vega NM. 2024. Maximum likelihood estimators for colony-forming units. Microbiology Spectrum 12(9):e03946-23. https://doi.org/10.1128/spectrum.03946-23

Overview

The goal of CFUestimatoR is to accurately and precisely estimate the density of CFUs from plate counts while accounting for different sources of error (sample fluctuation, colony crowding, pipetting) during the sampling process, without discarding or losing valuable data.

CFUestimatoR offers two estimators: 1) A Poisson estimator with a user-set crowding cutoff. Note: this function can alos compute the “naive” Poisson estimator by setting the thresholding value MM to Inf and 2) a maximum likelihood estimator (default) based on the most probable number approach that explicitely models the process of crowding.

Poisson

The Poisson model is arguably the most common model for calculating CFUs. Poisson assumes the number of colonies on a plate are Poison distributed with variation from sampling and that the mean colony count is equal to the variance. The most likely estimator under this model is just the ratio of the total number of colonies counted across all plates divided by the total amount of liquid plated.

$$ r_{\text{mle}} = \frac{\underset{k}{\sum} n_{k}}{V \underset{k}{\sum} d_{k}} = \frac{\underset{k}{\sum} n_{k}}{\underset{k}{\sum} V_{k}} , \sigma = \frac{r_{\text{mle}\&\text{nbsp};}}{\\sqrt{\underset{k}{\sum} n_{k}}} $$

One weakness with this approach is that it cannot account for the event where two individual cells land on a small enough area that they grow together and are only countable as a single colony. The paper refers to this process as “crowding.”

The Poisson model can control for crowding by incorporating a user-defined thresholding value MM, below which it is assumed crowding is negligable and does not need to be modeled. This results in the following estimator.

$$ r_{\text{mle}\textrm{ }} = \frac{\underset{k}{\sum} I ⁡ n_{k} \leq M ⁢ n_{k}}{\underset{k}{\sum} I ⁡ n_{k} \leq M ⁢ V_{k}} , \sigma = \frac{r_{m ⁢ l ⁢ e}}{\\sqrt{\underset{k}{\sum} I ⁡ n_{k} \leq M ⁢ n_{k}}} $$

In practive the cutoff number NN should be set to a number less than when crowding starts to be important. This is equivalent to the TNTC (“too numerous to count”) value commonly used in microbiology. A good default value is N=300N = 300

MLE

The MLE estimator is slightly more complicated. Here a plate is divided into N≈AplateAcolo⁢nyN \approx \frac{A_{\text{plate}}}{A_{\text{colo⁢ny}}} regions, with each region the size of a full colony. We make the assumptions that if more than one cell lands on region NiN_{i}, the colonies that form from these cells will grow together and be counted as one colony. For each region, the number of cells landing in that region will be Poisson distributed with parameter λ=dkrVN\lambda = \frac{d_{k} r V}{N}.

In the paper the authors show how this framing is equivalent to the MPN approach and requires three paramters 1) the total NkN_k virtual MPN tubes tested, 2) the dilution volume from the original sample VkV_k, and 3) the number nkn_k of virtual tubes that are positive for growth.

Basically, the probability of nkn_k successes in region NiN_i is describable from a binomial distribution where the probability of zero cells at region NiN_i is p0=e−dkrV/Nip_{0} = e^{- d_{k} r V / N_i} while the probability of ≥1\geq 1 landing in region NiN_i is p>=e−dkrV/Nip_{\gt} = e^{- d_{k} r V / N_i} resulting in the expression

pnk=(Nnk)p>nkp0N−nk=(Nnk)(1−e−dkrVN)nke−dkrVN−nk p n_{k} = \binom{N}{n_k} p_{>}^{n_{k}} p_{0}^{N - n_{k}} = \binom{N}{n_k} ( 1 - e^{- \frac{d_{k} r V}{N}} )^{n_{k}} e^{- d_{k} r V N - n_{k} }

where the MLE density can be found form solving the following eqation for rr

∑kdknkN(1−e−rdkV/N)=∑kdk \underset{k}{\sum} \frac{d_{k} n_{k}}{N(1 - e^{- r d_{k} V / N})} = \underset{k}{\sum} d_{k}

When using this estimator in practice we must choose a value for the Estimated Maximum Colony Number (NN). A good starting estimate here is the ratio of the area of the plate to the average colony size, which for a standard 100 mm petri dish is N=5000N=5000

Using the estimators

Choosing N

Method Meaning of N Default
"mle" Estimated Maximum Colony Number. (I.e., N perfectly packed colonies fit on a plate) 5000
"poisson" Counts at or above N are excluded 300
  • The cutoff number in the Poisson approach should be a number less than when crowding starts to be important on the plate.
  • For "mle", a good starting estimate is the ratio of the area of the plate to the average colony size. Any count above N gives an estimate of Inf.

Note: sometimes you may use a drop-spotting approach (e.g., Miles and Misra) if you have miniaturized your assay. For example if you’ve plated a 2 μl spot then a value of 50 is a good choice. In general, the drop spotting approach will usually produce noisier data.

One sample at a time

The estimators work directly on vectors of counts and dilutions. Here are three replicates at each of three dilutions. Setting V = 1 returns CFU in the volume plated (i.e., no back calculation to concentration in the original sample).

dilution <- rep(c(1e-7, 1e-6, 1e-5), each = 3)
count <- c(5, 8, 4, 62, 77, 51, 456, 597, 356)

find_mle(count, dilution, N = 5000, V = 1)
#>          r  stderr         type
#> 1 50741067 1262704 ML_estimator

The Poisson estimator discards counts at or above N, which protects against crowded plates. Here the three plates at the 1e-5 dilution (counts of 356 to 597) are excluded, so only the six plates at 1e-7 and 1e-6 are used.

find_poisson_cutoff(count, dilution, N = 300, V = 1)
#>          r  stderr           type
#> 1 62727273 4359847 poisson_cutoff

Setting N = Inf includes all observations (even those with very high colony counts) and gives the naive Poisson estimate from the paper.

find_poisson_cutoff(count, dilution, N = Inf, V = 1)
#>          r  stderr           type
#> 1 48528529 1207192 poisson_cutoff

The naive estimate is lower than the cutoff estimate because colonies on crowded plates are undercounted. The maximum likelihood estimator uses all the data and models the saturation, so it needs no cutoff but it does need a sensible N.

Many samples all together

estimate_cfu() applies one estimator to every group in a data frame. The bundled example data has one row per plate.

path <- system.file("extdata", "cfu_example.tsv", package = "CFUestimatoR")
cfu <- read.delim(path)
head(cfu)
#>              measurement time_hours growth_media sample_or_strain replicate
#> 1 starting-density check          0          PPY            1977A         a
#> 2 starting-density check          0          PPY            1977A         b
#> 3 starting-density check          0          PPY            1977A         a
#> 4 starting-density check          0          PPY            1977A         b
#> 5 starting-density check          0      PPY+Str            1977E         a
#> 6 starting-density check          0      PPY+Str            1977E         b
#>   dilution vol_plated_ml colony_count
#> 1    1e-06           0.1          337
#> 2    1e-06           0.1          259
#> 3    1e-07           0.1           40
#> 4    1e-07           0.1           44
#> 5    1e-06           0.1          341
#> 6    1e-06           0.1          391

Name the count column with count (the dilution column is dilution here, which is the default). Use group to say which columns define a sample. Leaving replicate out of group pools replicates.

estimate_cfu(
  cfu,
  count = colony_count,
  group = c(measurement, time_hours, growth_media, sample_or_strain),
  N = 5000,
  sampling_vol = vol_plated_ml
)
#>               measurement time_hours growth_media sample_or_strain    estimator
#> 1          direct plating         48          PPY               E1 ML_estimator
#> 2          direct plating         48          PPY               E2 ML_estimator
#> 3          direct plating         48      PPY+Str               E1 ML_estimator
#> 4          direct plating         48      PPY+Str               E2 ML_estimator
#> 5 SGT calibration plating         48      PPY+Str          control ML_estimator
#> 6  starting-density check          0          PPY            1977A ML_estimator
#> 7  starting-density check          0      PPY+Str            1977E ML_estimator
#>       CFU_ml CFU_ml_stderr
#> 1 1469416498      82274187
#> 2 2154889790      99937499
#> 3  360327325      40540075
#> 4  589537227      51906132
#> 5 2117968546     110561892
#> 6 3179163302     121933373
#> 7 3891949271     135366618

sampling_vol is always in ml and defaults to 0.1 (100 ul), which is the standard volume plated on a 100 mm petri dish. It can be a single number or, as here, a column giving the volume plated for each row (e.g. vol_plated_ml). Note: The volume must be constant within each group!

Choose the Poisson estimator with method = "poisson", where N is now the cutoff:

estimate_cfu(
  cfu,
  count = colony_count,
  group = c(sample_or_strain, growth_media),
  method = "poisson",
  N = 500,
  sampling_vol = vol_plated_ml
)
#>   sample_or_strain growth_media      estimator     CFU_ml CFU_ml_stderr
#> 1            1977A          PPY poisson_cutoff 3090909091     118530953
#> 2            1977E      PPY+Str poisson_cutoff 3759090909     130716399
#> 3          control      PPY+Str poisson_cutoff 2085227273     108847978
#> 4               E1          PPY poisson_cutoff 1450000000      81184414
#> 5               E1      PPY+Str poisson_cutoff  359090909      40400884
#> 6               E2          PPY poisson_cutoff 2113636364      98017539
#> 7               E2      PPY+Str poisson_cutoff  586363636      51626440

Notes:

  • group accepts any tidyselect expression, e.g. group = c(sample_or_strain, growth_media), starts_with("treat") or where(is.character). Omit it for no grouping.
  • The count and dilution columns default to count and dilution. Pass count and dilution a column name from your data if yours differ, e.g. count = colony_count.
